openingProblem.problem: In 1950 Chinese and American soldiers fought each other in Korea, and China was the Soviet Union's partner. In 1979 the US recognised the People's Republic and the two cooperated against the USSR. How did China change sides?

chunks.title: Allies and enemies: the triangle takes shape, 1949–1958
chunks.body:
When **Mao Zedong** proclaimed the People's Republic of China (PRC) on 1 October 1949, the Soviet Union, not America, was his partner. The Soviets had helped the Chinese Communists at a crucial moment: after Japan's surrender they occupied Manchuria and left only when Communist forces were in place to take it. The United States, by contrast, had backed Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists. It suspended relations with the new state, and for thirty years it recognised Chiang's government on Taiwan as the government of all China.

The **Korean War** turned estrangement into enmity. When the war broke out in June 1950, the US sent its Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait, and when Chinese troops entered the war in late 1950, American and Chinese soldiers fought each other. Washington imposed an embargo on China and worked to isolate Peking.

Taiwan remained the flashpoint. In September 1954 the PRC began shelling the offshore islands of Jinmen and Mazu, held by the Nationalists. The US signed a Mutual Defense Treaty with Taiwan, Congress authorised Eisenhower to defend it, and the administration considered options up to the use of nuclear weapons. The crisis eased when Zhou Enlai, at the Bandung Conference in April 1955, offered to negotiate. From August 1955 American and Chinese ambassadors met, first in Geneva and later in Warsaw. In sixteen years and 136 meetings they agreed only on the return of stranded citizens, because the status of Taiwan blocked everything else. Yet the talks gave the two enemies a channel through which misunderstandings could be prevented from becoming war. A second crisis over the islands in 1958 ended when the US re-supplied the garrisons.

There were early signs of strain on the Communist side too. When Khrushchev denounced Stalin in February 1956, Chinese leaders expressed grave doubts about his reforms.

This mattered because in the 1950s China was the junior partner of the USSR and the open enemy of the US, which meant that any change in either relationship would transform the balance of the Cold War.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The ambassadorial talks kept a channel open.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Taiwan was the central obstacle to any US-China accommodation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Repatriation of nationals was agreed in 1955.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Sino-Soviet partnership already showed strains by 1956.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The USSR had helped the Communists win in Manchuria.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Hostility between the US and the PRC was caused above all by the Korean War, which made them direct military enemies.
useItInAnEssay.prove: When the war broke out in June 1950 the US sent the Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait, and after China entered the war in late 1950 Washington imposed an embargo and worked to isolate Peking.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the question of Taiwan, already unresolved since 1949, became tied to a war, so Chinese attacks on the offshore islands in 1954 and 1958 brought new crises.

chunks.title: The Sino-Soviet split, 1956–1966
chunks.body:
The partnership between the two Communist giants broke apart within a decade. A US National Intelligence Estimate of December 1966 summed up American understanding of why. Serious but hidden differences had existed even under Stalin, and open antagonism dated back "at least to 1960". Underlying everything were conflicts of national interest: old Russian and Chinese rivalry in Mongolia and Korea, and a newer rivalry for leadership of the Communist world. Differences in wealth and power, doctrinal quarrels over Communist strategy and even personal hatred between Khrushchev and Mao all played a part.

Two moves in the late 1950s gave the dispute its own momentum, according to the estimate: the Soviet Union's refusal to give China the means to build nuclear weapons, and Peking's decision to challenge Moscow's dominance of the bloc. The break had real costs for China. In April 1961 US intelligence reported that the dislocations of Mao's "Great Leap Forward" and "the removal of Soviet technicians" had disrupted China's industrialisation; industrial growth had fallen from about 33 per cent in 1959 to 16 per cent in 1960. China pressed on alone and exploded its own atomic bomb in 1964.

By the mid-1960s each side denounced the other in public. China accused the Soviet Union of collusion with the US and of turning itself into a "bourgeois society"; Moscow replied that Chinese policies had "nothing in common with Marxism-Leninism". The Vietnam War added urgency, because Soviet supplies for North Vietnam had to cross China. In March 1969 another US estimate judged that Mao's "ideological pretensions" had earned China the enmity of the USSR and that, while Mao remained in charge, he would be "an insurmountable obstacle" to any accommodation with Moscow.

Was the split about ideology or national interest? The US analysts' answer was both: ideological rivalry over who led world Communism was itself a struggle for power, while disputes over nuclear weapons, borders and aid were matters of national interest.

This mattered because the Communist world was no longer a single bloc, which meant that the United States might one day play the two Communist powers against each other.

chunks.title: 1969: border war and the opening to America
chunks.body:
In March 1969 the hostility turned violent. Soviet and Chinese troops fought **armed clashes on the Ussuri River**, on their shared frontier. In August 1969 a US National Intelligence Estimate wrote that "for the first time, it is reasonable to ask whether a major Sino-Soviet war could break out". The Soviets, it noted, had a reason to strike soon rather than later: China's emerging nuclear force. The analysts saw "some chance" that Moscow might attack China's nuclear and missile sites. They concluded that the Chinese now regarded the USSR as their "most immediate enemy", while Moscow wanted better relations with the West in order to "contain" China.

The new American president saw an opportunity. In March 1969 Richard Nixon told President de Gaulle that in the long run the US should recognise both China and the Soviet Union as great powers and build "parallel relationships" with them. Both sides now had reasons to talk. For Washington, mired in Vietnam, better relations with Peking might undermine Communist alliances, isolate North Vietnam and increase American leverage over the Soviet Union. For Mao, fear of the USSR made the US a useful counterweight.

The approach was cautious and secret. Nixon eased travel and trade restrictions dating from the Korean War, the ambassadorial talks resumed in 1969, and he opened a secret channel through Pakistan's President Yahya Khan. Mao told the American journalist Edgar Snow that he would be happy to talk with Nixon. In April 1971, after American and Chinese table-tennis players had fraternised at a competition in Japan, China invited the US team to visit: "Ping Pong Diplomacy" gave a public face to the secret negotiations. Henry Kissinger, Nixon's National Security Adviser, flew to Beijing twice in 1971, the first time in complete secrecy. In October 1971 the United Nations voted to give China's seat to the PRC in place of Taiwan, a major diplomatic triumph for Peking.

This mattered because the border war made the USSR China's main enemy, which meant that the two former foes, China and the United States, now shared an interest in balancing Soviet power.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The analysts did not expect China to attack the USSR.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Vietnam was also a major US motive.

chunks.title: From Beijing to normalisation, 1972–1979
chunks.body:
From 21 to 28 February 1972 Richard Nixon visited China, the first American president to visit the mainland while in office, and met Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai. The visit ended with the **Shanghai Communiqué**, in which each side stated its position on Taiwan. The PRC affirmed that Taiwan was part of China. The US "acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain that there is but one China", did not challenge that position and said it would withdraw its remaining troops from Taiwan. Mao and Zhou made clear that there could be no full normalisation while the US kept formal relations with Taiwan. In the Office of the Historian's judgement, rapprochement "fundamentally altered the context of the Cold War" and influenced the move towards détente with the Soviet Union. Nixon's aim, in his own phrase, was to give Moscow and Beijing "bigger fish to fry" than support for North Vietnam, though both continued to supply Hanoi.

Progress then slowed. The two countries opened liaison offices in each other's capitals in 1973, while Taiwan still had an embassy in Washington, and the US gradually withdrew its military personnel from Taiwan. But the Watergate scandal frustrated Nixon's hopes of full normalisation, and under Gerald Ford the fall of South Vietnam and conservative opposition made any move that looked like abandoning an anti-Communist ally politically dangerous.

**Jimmy Carter** completed the process. Carter's officials debated how to normalise relations without damaging relations with the Soviet Union, but decided the opportunity might not last. On 15 December 1978 the two governments announced that they would establish diplomatic relations from 1 January 1979. The US recognised the PRC as the sole legal government of China, ended its 1954 defence treaty with Taiwan and kept only unofficial ties with the island. In January 1979 Deng Xiaoping visited the US, where he informed Carter of China's plan to attack Vietnam. Congress passed the Taiwan Relations Act in April, promising Taiwan defensive arms, which angered Beijing. After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, Sino-American military cooperation increased.

This mattered because by 1979 China had moved from the Soviet camp to cooperation with the US, which meant that the Cold War had become a triangle in which the Soviet Union faced two hostile powers.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: China and the USSR continued to support North Vietnam.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Liaison offices worked as de facto embassies from 1973.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent was ideology the main cause of the Sino-Soviet split between 1956 and 1969?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Whether ideology outweighed national interest and personal rivalry

modelPlan.thesis: Ideology was the language of the split, but national interest and the contest for leadership drove it, as the Soviet refusal of nuclear help and the border clashes show.

arguments.claim: Ideology: rival claims to lead world Communism (named factor first).
National interest: nuclear weapons and aid.
Personal enmity and Mao's leadership.
Borders: the 1969 clashes.

modelPlan.counter: Chinese doubts about Khrushchev's de-Stalinisation in 1956 show that doctrine mattered from the start.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: What made compromise impossible? National interest, because disputes over nuclear help and borders could not be settled by doctrine.

segments.text: Ideology was the language of the Sino-Soviet split, but not its main cause.

A US estimate of 1966 noted that each side called the other a betrayal of Marxism-Leninism, but listed conflicts of national interest and the Soviet refusal to help China build nuclear weapons as the deeper causes.
This meant that ideological polemics expressed a struggle for power, so neither side could compromise without accepting the other's leadership.
However, Chinese doubts about de-Stalinisation in 1956 show that doctrine mattered from the start.
Ideology was therefore a real but secondary cause; the split was a contest for power fought in ideological terms.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Sino-Soviet split was the main reason for the rapprochement between the United States and China.” Discuss with reference to the period 1969 to 1979.
essayQuestions.scope: China, the US and the USSR

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: the split was the main reason
decodeKey.judgement: Whether the split outweighed Vietnam and other US motives

modelPlan.thesis: The split was the main reason China sought rapprochement and made it possible for both sides, but American motives in Vietnam and Nixon's search for 'parallel relationships' explain why Washington moved when it did.

arguments.claim: For: the USSR as China's main enemy after 1969.
For: cooperation against the USSR by 1979.
Against: US motives in Vietnam.
Against: Nixon's wider strategy of parallel relationships.

modelPlan.counter: Taiwan, not the USSR, decided the pace of normalisation between 1972 and 1979.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without the split would rapprochement have happened? Probably not, so it was the necessary condition.

segments.text: The Sino-Soviet split was the main reason for the rapprochement, because it made the USSR China's main enemy.
After the Ussuri clashes of March 1969, US analysts judged that China saw the USSR as its 'most immediate enemy', and by 1979 China and the US cooperated against the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
This meant that Mao needed a counterweight to Moscow, so he responded to Nixon's approaches through Pakistan and ping-pong diplomacy.
However, the US had its own motives: officials hoped to isolate North Vietnam and gain leverage over the USSR, and Nixon sought 'parallel relationships' with both Communist powers.
The split was therefore the necessary condition of rapprochement, while American aims explain its timing.

essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for hostility between the United States and the People's Republic of China between 1949 and 1958.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Hostility rested on US non-recognition after 1949, was turned into enmity by the Korean War, and was kept alive by the unresolved question of Taiwan, though both sides avoided all-out war.

arguments.claim: Non-recognition after 1949.
The Korean War and the embargo.
Taiwan and the Strait crises.
Limits: the ambassadorial talks.

modelPlan.counter: The talks from 1955 show that both sides wanted to avoid war.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? Korea, because it made the two direct military enemies.

segments.text: Hostility between the US and the PRC was caused above all by the Korean War.
When the war began in June 1950 the US sent the Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait, and after China entered the war it imposed an embargo and worked to isolate Peking.
This meant that the unresolved question of Taiwan became tied to a war, so the PRC's shelling of the offshore islands in 1954 and 1958 produced new crises.
However, both sides avoided all-out war, and the ambassadorial talks from August 1955 kept a channel open.
Korea therefore turned estrangement into enmity, while Taiwan kept the hostility alive.

essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of the Sino-US rapprochement for superpower relations between 1971 and 1979.
essayQuestions.scope: China, the US and the USSR

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far it changed the structure of the Cold War

modelPlan.thesis: The rapprochement was highly significant because it turned a two-bloc contest into a triangle that left the USSR facing two hostile powers; but Taiwan and Vietnam limited cooperation until 1979.

arguments.claim: The 1972 visit 'fundamentally altered the context'.
Influence on US-Soviet détente.
Normalisation and cooperation against the USSR.
Limits: Vietnam and Taiwan.

modelPlan.counter: Both Communist powers kept supplying North Vietnam, so the triangle did not end Cold War conflict in Asia.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By what criterion? The structure of the Cold War: after 1972 it was no longer a contest between two blocs.

segments.text: The rapprochement was highly significant because it changed the structure of the Cold War.
Nixon's visit of February 1972 produced the Shanghai Communiqué, and on 1 January 1979 the US and PRC established diplomatic relations.
This meant that the USSR faced two hostile powers, so rapprochement influenced the move towards US-Soviet détente.
However, Moscow and Beijing continued to supply Hanoi, and Taiwan delayed normalisation for seven years.
Rapprochement was therefore decisive for the Cold War's structure, if not for every regional conflict.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Sino-Soviet border clashes between 1969 and 1972.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The clashes grew from a decade of rivalry for leadership and from territorial and nuclear fears; their main consequence was that China, now seeing the USSR as its chief enemy, turned to the United States.

arguments.claim: Cause: the long rivalry for leadership.
Cause: Soviet fear of China's nuclear force.
Consequence: fear of a major war.
Consequence: rapprochement with the US.

modelPlan.counter: China's turn to the US also needed American willingness, which came from Vietnam and Nixon's strategy.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The Sino-US alignment, which by 1979 had become cooperation against the USSR.

segments.text: The border clashes grew from a decade of rivalry and from Soviet fear of China's nuclear force.
A US estimate of August 1969 noted that the emerging Chinese nuclear threat gave the Soviets reasons to strike soon, and saw 'some chance' of an attack on China's nuclear sites.
This meant that China now saw the USSR as its most immediate enemy, so it sought a counterweight in the US, inviting the American table-tennis team in April 1971.
However, the rapprochement also depended on American motives in Vietnam and Nixon's search for 'parallel relationships'.
The clashes were therefore the turning point that made the Sino-US rapprochement possible.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast Sino-Soviet and Sino-US relations between 1949 and 1979.
essayQuestions.scope: China, the US and the USSR

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: The two relationships moved in opposite directions: from partnership to armed conflict with the USSR, and from war to cooperation with the US; in both, national interest mattered more than ideology.

arguments.claim: Similarity: national interest decided both.
Similarity: each passed through armed conflict.
Difference: opposite directions over time.
Difference: ideology bound and then divided the Communist pair.

modelPlan.counter: Even by 1979 China criticised the US as too conciliatory to the USSR, so cooperation had limits.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? The direction of change, which turned the Cold War into a triangle.

segments.text: China's relations with the two superpowers moved in opposite directions between 1949 and 1979.
China fought the US in Korea in 1950, whereas it clashed with Soviet troops on the Ussuri in 1969; by 1979 it had diplomatic relations with the US and saw the USSR as its main enemy.
This meant that ideology, which had first bound China to Moscow, gave way to national interest, which drew it towards Washington.
However, both relationships were shaped by the same forces of security and power, and China remained wary of the US, criticising it in 1979 as too conciliatory to Moscow.
The decisive difference was therefore the direction of change, which reshaped the Cold War.
